title: Contextualising the Structural Efficacy of Top-Down Strategic Research Plans in Higher Education: The SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
The expansion of corporate management models within higher education institutions over the past several decades has completely transformed how academic knowledge is produced, evaluated, and incentivised. Modern universities have increasingly transitioned away from traditional collegial governance structures toward managerial frameworks, commonly known as New Public Management (NPM). Under this corporate paradigm, senior university administration relies on institutional strategic research plans, formal performance indicators, and centralised accountability metrics to align faculty behaviours with broader organisational objectives. This literature review synthesises recent international scholarship on academic managerialism to contextualise a core underlying question: do strategic research plans work? By examining the mechanisms of administrative steering, institutional leadership capabilities, and individual faculty responses, this review establishes the conceptual and empirical baseline from which this evaluative research question extends.


The introduction of corporate steering in public research sectors is frequently framed as a necessary mechanism to increase operational efficiency and institutional accountability. Scholars examining the Central and Eastern European contexts demonstrate that department heads are forced to act as primary mediators, negotiating the intense friction between emerging corporate managerial expectations and traditional academic autonomy (Machovcova, Zabrodska, and Mudrak 2019). This systemic transition shifts the focus of the university from an open site of unconstrained intellectual inquiry to a managed environment where output must be quantified and regularised. Empirical observations on the long-term impacts of NPM suggest that while these policy instruments are designed to stimulate public research efficiency, they frequently function as a double-edged sword, creating administrative inflation and narrow publishing strategies among faculty (Schubert 2009).
Furthermore, the global reach of these corporate practices is evident across diverse higher education landscapes, including developing regions such as the United Arab Emirates, where new managerialism is actively deployed to reshape institutional reputations (Ajayan and Balasubramanian 2020). When fiscal cutbacks occur, the pressure to maintain research performance becomes even more acute; institutions are forced to sustain or accelerate output levels even when financial incentives and direct support lines are actively declining(Bak and Kim 2023). This environments implies that corporate management systems are often entrenched as total quality management tools, operating on the corporate premise that academic institutions are structurally no different from any commercial enterprise and can therefore be optimised through identical auditing and performance-monitoring systems(Hasham 2018). Consequently, the historical evolution of research performance measurement systems, particularly within heavily evaluated sectors like Australian higher education, outlines a steady intensification of administrative oversight designed to align local work with corporate parameters (Martin-Sardesai et al. 2019).



A central tenet of corporate strategic planning is that institutional leadership possesses the causal power to steer university performance toward explicit benchmarks of research excellence. Recent quantitative modeling of presidential capabilities in Chinese higher education argues that specific strategic competencies at the executive level correlate positively with institutional performance gains and international visibility (Dong, Wu, and Yu 2025). Similarly, evaluations of academic leadership and university performance across European and Russian frameworks investigate whether universities demonstrate measurable improvements when led by active, highly cited scholars who embody research excellence, rather than pure career administrators (Gerashchenko 2022). This structural steering is frequently reinforced by regional contagion effects, where the strategic choices and performance trajectories of neighbouring peer institutions create a powerful normative pressure that drives local academic leadership to adopt identical strategic management models (Saftiuc, Proscanu, and Teodorescu 2025).
For these administrative plans to translate into concrete scholarly output, university leaders place immense emphasis on building an institutional shared vision that attempts to bridge the historical divide between research and teaching mandates(Bui et al. 2024). Senior management relies on transformational leadership styles, operating under the assumption that inspiring a collective corporate identity will foster internal creativity and accelerate high-impact innovation outputs (Salim and Zakaria 2021). In fields such as green innovation and technology transfer, evidence indicates that the specific academic and corporate experiences of the top management team can significantly shape the volume and direction of institutional innovation outputs (Zhao et al. 2021). Moreover, when academic executives retain active boardroom connections, they can directly couple lab-based research with high-impact industrial commercialisation, demonstrating how top-down strategies attempt to steer basic science toward applied economic utility (Zhu, Wu, and Gaidai 2025).



At the individual level, the primary mechanisms used to enforce strategic alignment are institutional incentives, formal performance appraisals, and individual research productivity tracking. Extensive evidence reviews regarding how individual research productivity is managed within academic organisations show that while structured interventions can alter short-term output counts, they rarely change long-term scholarly trajectories (Ryazanova and Jaskiene 2022). The implementation of routine institutional bibliometric reports is frequently positioned as a tool for responsible metric scenarios, yet in practice, these data summaries often function as coercive monitoring mechanisms that hold individual faculty accountable to generic performance targets(Cabezas-Clavijo and Torres-Salinas 2021). To systematically map these dynamics, advanced institutional frameworks have emerged, such as bibliometric strength, potential, and risk analysis models, which allow administrators to track exactly how faculty publication choices respond to central strategic choices and funding pathways (Iping et al. 2024).
The efficacy of these incentive structures remains highly dependent on localized professional contexts and personal scholarly investments. In Canada, broad empirical studies of primary care researchers demonstrate that productivity is strongly associated with protected research time, dedicated infrastructure, and targeted team-based funding rather than purely top-down corporate mandates (Aggarwal et al. 2024). Furthermore, the specialized nature of research production is heavily reliant on specific cognitive resources and long-term personal investments, which means that arbitrary administrative redirections can result in severe cognitive friction and operational inefficiency for the scholar(Degli Antoni, Fia, and Sacconi 2022). Quantitative analyses of individual academic research agendas confirm that broader organizational factors and centralized institutional priorities interact directly with disciplinary traditions, meaning that top-down steering tools must constantly compete with an academic’s internalized scholarly values and international peer networks (Horta and Santos 2020).



The imposition of intensive corporate performance management has generated deep structural tensions, with many scholars arguing that these frameworks actively stifle academic freedom and distort genuine knowledge production. Critical discourse analyses highlight that aggressive performance management frameworks force a precarious state of affairs upon academic work, transforming scholarly writing into a rushed commodity designed to satisfy auditing cycles rather than solve profound intellectual problems (Morrish and Sauntson 2016). This shift creates a deep sense of alienation, where academic identities are systematically reconfigured to fit the parameters of the managed university, sparking widespread subtle resistance among faculty who seek to protect their professional autonomy from neoliberal encroachment (Morrish 2017). In specialized fields like social work education, the imposition of a marketized, neo-liberal agenda is shown to directly compromise the critical, social-justice mission of the discipline by prioritizing commercial metric capture over community engagement (MacDonald and Nixon 2016).
The human cost of these auditing regimes is captured in extreme qualitative terms by academics who describe the modern pressure cooker environment, noting that a scholar without constant high-impact publications is treated with systemic irrelevance within the new times of hyper-competition (Xu and Poole 2024). This creates intense institutional struggles for recognition where individual departments are pitted against one another for scarce resources, fragmenting the university’s traditional community of scholars(Muench and Baier 2012). When university governance attempts to forcefully mandate new socio-political or operational directions, such as institutional sustainability, teachers’ perspectives frequently expose a profound disconnect; the formal policies and administrative structures lack meaningful faculty buy-in because they are perceived as top-down compliance exercises rather than authentic scholarly transformations (Castro-Gomez et al. 2026). Without aligning internal policy incentives directly with the intrinsic motivations and professional values of the faculty, centralized administrative mandates fail to cultivate genuine participation or sustainable scholarly growth (Barsallo et al. 2026).



This breief review on higher education management demonstrates a persistent and unresolved conflict between top-down corporate steering and bottom-up faculty behaviour. While institutional theories and administrative models posit that clear leadership capabilities, shared corporate visions, and targeted bibliometric monitoring can successfully optimize and direct an institution’s research performance, critical empirical accounts expose widespread resistance, strategic gaming, and profound alignment failures. This profound contradiction exposes a major gap in evaluative scientometrics: we lack robust, objective, longitudinal measures of whether corporate university strategies genuinely shape the intellectual landscape of an institution or if they merely retroactively rebrand pre-existing, faculty-driven strengths. It is precisely from this critical juncture that our primary research question extends: do strategic research plans work? By applying longitudinal correspondence analysis and bibliometric co-citation mapping across distinct planning eras, this project moves past qualitative perceptions to provide an empirical verdict on the structural power of corporate university mandates by relying on the research corpus of Saint Mary’s University (SMU).

The distributions in tables @ref(tab:topvenuespersc) and @ref(tab:sourcediversity) suggests a regional, mid-sized research profile that leans on national publishing avenues to maintain visibility in the social sciences, humanities, and professional fields, while demonstrating a highly concentrated, globally competitive footprint in select natural sciences. We can see this in the large volume of publications in Astronomy & Astrophysics (262 papers in the Astrophysical Journal) and Physics (96 papers in Physical Review C). This pattern highlights an institutional centre of excellence. Despite its smaller size, SMU hosts the Institute for Computational Astrophysics (ICA) and the primary regional centre for astronomical data analytics and numerical simulation, enabling its faculty to lead high-impact, internationally co-authored projects using high-performance computing clusters and advanced observatories. This specialized structural investment explains why fields like astronomy and physics accumulate exceptionally high publication counts: international citation database indexing models have a strong affinity for these types of intensive scientific networks. Other core natural sciences also demonstrate strong clusters of activity but tend to utilise national dissemination channels, as seen in Geology (80 papers in the Canadian Journal of Earth Sciences) and Chemistry (43 papers in the Canadian Journal of Chemistry). Similarly, the social sciences and humanities show a reliance on Canadian-specific journals. Venues like Canadian Psychology, the Canadian Journal of Development Studies, and the Canadian Journal of Administrative Sciences serve as primary outlets for this work. This pattern highlights how local scholars use national journals to publish peer-reviewed research that addresses regional or national matters. Finally, the low counts in fields like Sociology and Criminology reflect disciplinary conventions and indexing limitations of the WoS database rather than a lack of faculty output. These disciplines, in which authors frequently work alone or in very small co-author groups, rely on monographs, book chapters, and specialized local journals that are often under-represented in international citation indexes. This is evident, in some measure, by the fact that the top publication venues for Literature, Asian Studies, Philosophy, and Criminology & Penology are either regional journals (the Antigonish Review) or edited collections (Zen Conquests and Big Crime and Big Policing).
In a small Canadian university context, the steep drop in publication counts between our top fields and the rest is entirely unsurprising. This pattern reveals an institutional structure driven by a few intense pockets of significant research volume rather than a broad, uniform baseline across all departments. The top tiers are dominated by massive, internationally co-authored publications, while the lower tiers represent fields where scholarship is either more solitary or less well captured by Web of Science indexing. Generally speaking, these distributions remind us that while the database effectively captures our high-energy science clusters, it also requires careful contextual framing when evaluating the nationally focused and monograph-reliant output of the social sciences and humanities.

Number of Publications Across Time




The growth rate of the SMU-affiliated corpus for the time span under consideration was 6%, captured in Figure @ref(fig:pubsgrowthplot). There is a straightforward connection between this growth rate and the average document age of 14 years, noted in Table @ref(tab:maininformation). This connection is relevant because it helps highlight a distinct shift in our historical publication volume. First, this 6% expansion rate indicates that our total publication output is heavily skewed toward the modern end of our 36-year timeline. Because an exponential growth pattern inherently produces a dense concentration of recent work, I noted that the majority of our 7850 documents were published in the latter half of this tracking block. This surge of newer records effectively pulls the mathematical weight of the entire dataset toward the present day. Because of this compounding effect, our 6%, growth rate causes the university’s total publication volume to double roughly every 12 to 13 years.

title: Contextualising the Structural Efficacy of Top-Down Strategic Research Plans in Higher Education: The SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
Research Impact
Each publication was cited, on average, 24 times, suggesting that research at SMU is generally being recognized and built upon by other scholars. Importantly, however, when evaluating institutional research impact, raw average citation counts must be interpreted with caution. First, arithmetic means are easily distorted by a small number of highly cited publications, masking the reality that the majority of scholarly publications receive far fewer citations (Aria and Cuccurullo 2026). Second, cumulative citation counts suffer from an inherent temporal bias. Older publications have had significantly more time to accrue citations compared to recent works, regardless of their immediate influence. Addressing these structural biases requires examining the complete citation distribution alongside time-normalized metrics.
A density distribution curve (Figure @ref(fig:citationdensity)) is useful for this purpose because it maps the exact shape, spread, and skewness of citation counts across a continuous scale. Incorporating a log scale into this density plot is crucial because, as noted above, citation counts can span multiple orders of magnitude, ranging from uncited papers to highly cited outliers. On a standard linear axis, massive upper values compress the vast majority of citations with low or mid citation values into an unreadable spike near zero. By applying a logarithmic transformation each equal step on the axis represents an exponential increase (e.g., 0, 10, 100, 1000 citations). Furthermore, using \(\log_{10}(x + 1)\) prevents mathematical errors (\(\log_{10}(0) = -\infty\)) and preserves uncited work at the zero mark. This transformation spreads out the dense concentration of lower-cited papers while pulling extreme outliers into view, allowing us to evaluate the full spectrum of institutional output on a single, clear visual plane.





Citation Density




Data in Table @ref(tab:citationdistsummary) indicates that while each each publication received an average of 24 citations, the median value of 7 citations provides a far more accurate baseline for a typical document, reflecting the strong right-skewness of the dataset. A small subset of hyper-cited papers—reaching up to a maximum of 1771 citations—pulls the arithmetic mean upward. Furthermore, 21% of our total output (1632documents) remains uncited, while the middle 50% of publications spans an interquartile range of 22 citations. On our log-transformed scale, the distribution resolves into two distinct visual features: a primary mass of uncited and low-citation papers, followed by a broader secondary curve peaking near 9 citations before trailing off into a long tail of extreme outliers. This secondary peak represents a clear cohort effect driven by time, showing where mature, steady scholarship gradually settles after decades in circulation.

The citation velocity distribution mirrors and deepens the interpretation of global citation accumulation. While absolute volume favours older papers, citation velocity shifts the focus to immediate, contemporary relevance, pulling modern, rapid-growth publications to the forefront. When a paper shows a high absolute citation count but a relatively low citation velocity, it represents a mature classic paper with a stablized year-over-year influence that retains a large footprint because it has been indexed for decades. Conversely, a paper displaying a low absolute count but a large citation velocity represents a publication that creates immediate intellectual momentum. This dynamic is captured by the contrast between Mellier et al. (2025) and Wilkes and Zaworotko (1992). The 1992 ionic liquids paper has amassed 1,771 lifetime citations over more than three decades, yet its annual velocity is 50.60. Conversely, the 2025 Euclid mission overview registers only 454 global citations, but its citation velocity sits at 227, suggesting a significant contemporary publication.
Drawing on citation velocity bridges the gap between historical endurance and current intellectual momentum. Papers where both metrics are high can be understood as publications that continue to drive their fields forward. Foundational works, such as Wilkes and Zaworotko (1992) and Sharma and Vredenburg (1998), successfully maintain their positions in this velocity ranking because their compounding citation count totals are large enough to preserve a high annual speed even after decades of life. The work of Sharma and Vredenburg (1998) maintains a velocity of 57.93 alongside 1,680 total citations after nearly thirty years, suggesting that it is a highly resilient paper with which contemporary researchers still actively engage. Concurrently, the velocity metric elevates newer, highly targeted research such as Qaderi et al. (2023), which registers a relatively high velocity of 66.75 despite its recent publication, while also exposing how large-scale, multi-author networks like those of Aihara et al. (2018), Weaver et al. (2022), and Finkelstein et al. (2022) whose widespread institutional footprints allow for instant visibility that compresses traditional timelines. Ultimately, contrasting these differing scores illustrate that academic impact is driven by a range of factors, including, but not limited to, the network-accelerated speed of contemporary multi-author mega-projects and the steady, decade-long compounding pull of foundational texts.
Evaluating these metrics together underscores that relying solely on the average citation score overstates the typical impact across departments, demonstrating why measures such as the median and interquartile range are necessary to provide proper context for institutional research output. Outside these statistical strategies, contextualizing our findings against external benchmarks clarifies how our performance aligns with broader academic patterns. For example, Madison and Sundell (2022) conducted a study in Sweden to examine the publication and citation patterns of researchers across six disciplines related to health and social services. Using a total dataset of 959 active researchers over a ten-year observation window, they established that across all studied disciplines the average was 5.6 citations per publication. Their data revealed that a substantial portion of publications remained completely uncited, with 26% of all researchers failing to receive a single citation over the ten-year tracking period. This lack of scholarly impact was highly concentrated within specific fields, as the proportion of entirely uncited researchers ranged from 35% to 64% in the disciplines of education, sociology, and social work. Conversely, fields such as public health, psychology, and nursing demonstrated a far more robust international citation culture, with around 128 citations per researcher.
These structural disparities align directly with established bibliometric research on disciplinary cultures and communication media. In his foundational taxonomy of academic disciplines, Becher (1994) (see also Becher and Trowler (2001)) demonstrates that knowledge domains shape distinct research behaviours. “Hard-pure” sciences operate within tightly knit, competitive, research communities characterized by high publication rates and rapid citation velocity. Conversely, “soft-pure” disciplines—such as sociology, history, and the humanities—exhibit individualistic, loosely structured, and person-oriented frameworks with lower journal publication frequencies and alternative dissemination channels. As a result, applying uniform performance indicators across distinct academic units inherently advantages empirical hard sciences while penalizing soft applied and humanities fields.
Furthermore, as Larivière, Gringras, and Archambault (2006) highlight in their comparative analysis of Canadian researchers, bibliometric indexing databases introduce severe coverage biases between the Natural Sciences and Engineering (NSE) and the Social Sciences and Humanities (SSH). While journal articles account for nearly 80% of NSE research output, SSH scholarship relies far more heavily on monographs, book chapters, and national or regional publications. In the humanities, standard journal articles represent less than 35% of indexed documents, with book reviews comprising over 56% of database entries. Moreover, collaborative co-authorship—a primary driver of citation volume—nears 90% in NSE and 60% in social sciences, but remains a marginal phenomenon in the humanities at roughly 10%. Methodologically, these systemic field differences severely undermine the validity of relying on raw citation averages or restricted peer-review evaluation samples.
In their assessment of national research evaluation frameworks, Abramo and D’Angelo (2011) demonstrate that evaluating institutions based on limited subsets of “top” publications fails test robustness, as ranking outcomes fluctuate wildly depending on sample size and field-specific publication intensity. Because citation fertility varies radically between subject categories, raw institutional metrics fail to measure true productivity unless citation metrics are standardly evaluated across complete corpus distributions and normalized for field-specific citation density and document age.

text:
Scholarly Activity
A primary measure of authorial activity within bibliometrics is publication count. While raw publication counts offer a straightforward tally of productivity, relying on them introduces a structural flaw by overstating institutional output. In a standard raw frequency count, every listed contributor on a multi-authored paper receives an identical score of one, treating a solo-authored monograph and a mega-collaboration paper with hundreds of authors as mathematically equivalent units of credit. This approach obscures the collaborative density of the project and artificially inflates total publication counts across institutions when multi-authored papers are aggregated. Fractionalized counting directly addresses this distortion by allocating research credit proportionally among all co-authors of a single publication. The fractional method treats each publication as a single unit of value, dividing that unit equally by the total number of listed authors (\(1/N\)). By ensuring that the sum of all fractional shares for any given publication always equals exactly one per paper, this approach prevents the inflation inherent in raw counts and provides a far more accurate reflection of an author’s true relative contribution.
To illustrate this mechanism: suppose a researcher publishes three distinct papers within a specific institutional tracking block. If the first paper is a sole-authored study, the researcher retains full ownership and receives a fractional score of 1. If the second paper is a collaborative project written with a departmental colleague, the single point is divided equally, yielding a score of 0.5 for each participant. If the third paper is an international study featuring a large team of five co-authors, the division results in a fractional score of .2. Summing these individual values together results in a cumulative fractionalised publication score of 1.7 for that specific researcher, providing a normalised indicator of their individual contribution across different collaborative frameworks. Differently, absolute publicaiton counts registers a flat count every time an author’s name appears on a paper; the fractionalized score divides each paper by its total number of co-authors, meaning that a lower fractional ratio indicates high-density team collaboration. In bibliometric analysis, absolute frequency will always be higher than or equal to the fractionalized score. This occurs because a single publication carries a maximum credit value of 1.0; while every paper adds a full count of 1 to an author’s absolute total, any co-authored piece splits that single credit among all contributors, thereby reducing the fractionalized addition.

title: Contextualising the Structural Efficacy of Top-Down Strategic Research Plans in Higher Education: The SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
Section Summary
When examining the 36-year bibliometric profile of Saint Mary’s University, I observe an institutional footprint marked by significant growth and clear structural distinction. Our annual publication growth rate of 5.7% outpaces the historical global baseline of approximately 3%, reflecting an expanding research volume across our faculties. This output is firmly anchored in peer-reviewed journal publishing, with standard articles accounting for over 70% of our total production across 2,862 distinct sources. Furthermore, our overall output averages 23.8 citations per document—a figure that noticeably exceeds standard international disciplinary benchmarks—demonstrating that our work is actively utilized within the broader academic community.
However, relying solely on raw average citation counts can present a misleading impression of institutional performance. Arithmetic means are easily distorted by a small number of hyper-cited publications, masking the reality that the majority of documents receive far fewer citations. Across our corpus, while the mean citation count sits at 23.8, the median value of 7 provides a much more accurate baseline for a typical document, reflecting the strong right-skewness of the dataset where a few top papers reach up to 1,771 citations. Furthermore, 20.8% of our total output (1,632 documents) remains uncited, while the middle 50% of publications spans an interquartile range of 22 citations.
To map these distributions accurately, we evaluate density plots on logarithmic scales (\(\log_{10}(x + 1)\)), which spread out dense concentrations of lower-cited papers while keeping extreme outliers in view without dropping uncited documents. On a log scale, our raw citation distribution resolves into two main features: a primary mass of uncited and low-citation papers, followed by a secondary curve peaking near 9 citations. This secondary hump reflects a clear temporal bias, as older publications have had decades to passively accrue citations compared to recent works. To correct for this time bias, we analyze citation velocity—the average annual citation accumulation rate (\(\text{Current Year} - \text{Publication Year} + 1\)). Normalizing our corpus by age yields a mean velocity of 2.0 citations per year and a median velocity of 0.7. When age is controlled for, the secondary hump collapses into a steep peak near zero annual citations, revealing that a typical publication accrues engagement at a modest pace of under one citation per year, while a long tail reaching up to 227 citations per year isolates our high-energy contemporary projects.
Our data on authorship reveals a dual research culture that effectively balances expansive global collaboration with solitary scholarship. Our international co-authorship rate sits at 41.3%, with an average of nine co-authors per document, reflecting strong participation in international networks and multi-author projects. Concurrently, single-authored documents represent 22% of our corpus, showing that individual scholarship maintains a firm, stable position alongside large-scale collaborative frameworks.
Contextualizing these findings within scientometric literature clarifies how our performance aligns with broader academic patterns. As Madison and Sundell (2022) established in their population-based study of Swedish social service disciplines, average citation rates across applied social fields sit around 5.6 citations per publication, with 26% of researchers receiving zero citations over a ten-year window and uncited rates reaching 35% to 64% in education, sociology, and social work. These structural disparities align directly with Becher’s (1994) foundational taxonomy of academic disciplines. “Hard-pure” sciences operate within tightly knit, competitive, urban research communities with high publication rates and rapid citation velocity. Conversely, “soft-pure” disciplines—such as sociology, history, and the humanities—exhibit individualistic, loosely structured frameworks with lower journal publication frequencies and alternative dissemination channels.
Furthermore, as Larivière, Gingras, and Archambault (2006) highlight in their analysis of Canadian research, indexing databases like the Web of Science introduce severe coverage biases between the Natural Sciences and Engineering (NSE) and the Social Sciences and Humanities (SSH). While journal articles account for nearly 80% of NSE research output, SSH scholarship relies far more heavily on monographs, book chapters, and regional publications. In the humanities, standard journal articles represent less than 35% of indexed documents, with book reviews comprising over 56% of database entries. Moreover, collaborative co-authorship—a primary driver of citation volume—nears 90% in NSE and 60% in social sciences, but remains a marginal phenomenon in the humanities at roughly 10%.
Methodologically, these field differences demonstrate why evaluating institutional strength requires a highly nuanced approach. As Abramo and D’Angelo (2011) argue, evaluating institutions based on unadjusted raw averages or restricted sample subsets compromises assessment validity and robustness, as ranking outcomes fluctuate wildly depending on sample size and field-specific publication intensity. While hard science clusters in Astronomy, Astrophysics, and Physics drive rapid, network-accelerated output and high citation velocity, our humanities and social sciences reflect the steady, compounding impact of foundational independent work. Utilizing dual metrics—balancing total volume against fractionalized contributions, and cumulative totals against citation velocity—ensures that we evaluate our collective impact fairly across all academic traditions.
Finally, examining the distribution of publication types across our corpus provides concrete empirical confirmation of these broader structural dynamics. Standard peer-reviewed articles represent the primary driver of institutional volume, accounting for 5,649 documents (73.6% of total output). When combined with conference proceedings, meeting abstracts, and proceedings articles (738 documents), journal- and conference-centric scientific communications constitute over 83% of our overall footprint, capturing the operational norms of our natural and empirical science departments. Beneath this primary journal volume, a substantial secondary stream of humanistic and social science scholarship is evident in book reviews (529 items) and monograph chapters (405 items), which together account for over 12% of the total output. Minor editorial, correction, creative, data, and bibliographic document types comprise the remaining balance of under 4%. This distribution underscores an institutional research profile firmly grounded in international journal-based science, complemented by a steady, persistent tradition of monograph and review-based scholarship.

title: Keyword Co-occurance Analysis
text:
I use keyword co-occurrence analysis to examine the substantive organization of the SMU-affiliated corpus. The method belongs to the same broad family of bibliometric techniques as co-citation and co-author analysis, but its object is different: rather than asking which authors collaborate or which publications are cited together, it asks which research terms co-occur across a collection of publications. Authors and databases use keywords to characterize the content of a publication, typically identifying concepts, topics, methods, populations, objects of study, or research problems. The underlying assumption is that these terms are not distributed randomly. When two keywords repeatedly appear together in the same publications, that recurrence provides evidence that the ideas are being brought into relation within the literature. Co-word analysis therefore allows me to move from a collection of individual publications to a representation of the substantive relationships that recur across the corpus, without beginning from a predetermined classification of the literature.
A keyword co-occurrence network is constructed by first counting these relationships. In the simplified example, a co-occurrence matrix contains six research terms in its rows and columns, with each intersecting cell recording how many times a pair of terms appears together. Sport and Identity, for example, have a co-occurrence value of five, whereas Identity and Network Analysis co-occur only once.

The matrix is then converted into an undirected, weighted network using methods of network analysis. Each keyword becomes a node, and an edge connects two nodes when the corresponding keywords occur together in at least one publication. The weight of the edge records the frequency of that co-occurrence, allowing more recurrent relationships to be represented by thicker lines.
Once represented as a network, additional measures can be used to describe the position of individual terms and the structure of the network as a whole. Degree records the number of other keywords to which a term is directly connected, so a high-degree keyword is more extensively embedded in the network than one with relatively few connections. Community-detection algorithms such as Louvain identify groups of keywords that are more densely connected to one another than to the rest of the network.
Example Keyword Co-Occurrence Network
In the toy example, Masculinity, Sport, and Identity form one such group, while Network Analysis, Bibliometrics, and Data Science form another. The strongest relationships include Network Analysis–Bibliometrics (6), Sport–Identity (5), and Bibliometrics–Data Science (5). By contrast, the single co-occurrence between Identity and Network Analysis creates a comparatively weak bridge between the two communities. The visualization therefore makes both internal cohesion and cross-community connection visible. Spatial position should be interpreted cautiously, however, because it is partly a consequence of the layout algorithm rather than an independent substantive property.
What the resulting network reveals is not simply which keywords are common, but how the substantive vocabulary of a research corpus is organized relationally. Nodes identify the concepts present in the literature; degree indicates how broadly those concepts are connected; edge weights show which associations recur more or less frequently; and communities identify concentrations of terms that repeatedly occur together. When the highly connected terms within a community point toward a coherent substantive concern, those communities can reasonably be interpreted as research areas or thematic formations. The network can also identify bridging concepts that connect otherwise distinct areas of research and more peripheral terms that occupy specialized positions.

title: Keyword Co-occurance Analysis
text:
The SMU-affiliated keyword network
In what follows, I use keyword co-occurrence analysis to map recurring intellectual associations within the SMU-affiliated corpus of 7,850 publications. The network focuses on how the terms used to describe those publications are connected. Groups of densely connected keywords are represented as communities, but these communities should not be understood as predetermined departments, disciplines, or administrative categories. They are emergent groupings of concepts, research problems, methods, populations, and objects of study that recur together across the corpus. The resulting network therefore provides a way of examining both what SMU-affiliated researchers study and how different areas of research are related within the indexed literature.
A connection between two keywords indicates that the terms have been used together in describing the same scholarly output; it does not imply that they have the same meaning or necessarily belong to the same discipline. What matters analytically is the pattern of relationships among terms. A keyword may be highly connected because it appears alongside many different topics, while another may occupy a more specialized position because its connections are concentrated within a narrower area of research. The network is therefore best understood as a map of research association and connectedness rather than simply a count of topics.
The network combines two forms of keyword metadata. Author keywords are terms selected by authors to describe the subject matter of their publications, while database-generated keywords, such as Keywords Plus, are derived from information in the bibliographic record to identify additional topical relationships. These were combined before constructing the network to provide a broader representation of the subjects and concepts associated with each publication. As a result, a node labelled migration, galaxies, education, or another term represents a keyword in the bibliographic description of the corpus, not a researcher, department, publication, or project.
The vocabulary itself is heterogeneous. Some keywords identify broad substantive areas, while others refer to theoretical concepts, research methods, populations, geographic locations, objects of study, scientific processes, or highly specialized phenomena. Because author-supplied and database-generated keywords are combined, the network should be interpreted as a representation of how SMU research is bibliographically described and connected, rather than as a direct inventory of the concepts researchers themselves would necessarily identify as most important.

section: How to use the network and tables
text:
How to use the network and tables
The interactive network provides the broadest view of these relationships. Use the keyword search above the network to locate a particular term. Selecting a keyword highlights its node in yellow with a black border. Once selected, the nodes connected directly to that keyword are also highlighted. The network can then be zoomed and panned to bring these linked nodes into focus, and individual nodes may be dragged to make crowded areas easier to inspect. Moving a node changes only its position on the screen and does not alter the underlying network analysis.
When you look at a keyword together with all of its neighbours, you are looking at that keyword’s immediate local network. The selected keyword is the focal term, and each neighbour is another keyword that appeared with it in the metadata of at least one publication in the corpus. The neighbourhood therefore shows the set of topics, concepts, methods, populations, places, or objects of study that have been directly associated with that keyword in SMU-affiliated research. This neighbourhood can be interpreted as a picture of the keyword’s intellectual context. A keyword with neighbours drawn largely from its own community is embedded mainly within a relatively concentrated area of research. Selecting the keywords “behaviour”, “radial velocities”, “health”, “management history”, or “actor network theory” from the keyword drop down search menu offers an illustration of this type of pattern. A keyword whose neighbours span several communities may instead connect otherwise distinct areas of scholarly activity. Selecting the keywords “origin”, “sequence”, or “evolution” will illustrate this type of pattern.
Nodes with the same colour belong to the same intellectual community.1 Node size represents degree of connectedness: larger nodes are directly connected to a greater number of other keywords in the network, while smaller nodes have fewer direct connections and tend to occupy more specialized positions. Node size therefore represents network connectedness rather than the quality, importance, or volume of research associated with a keyword.
The tables provide complementary ways of examining the same network.

The Keyword neighbours table allows a reader to select an exact keyword and retrieve all of the terms directly connected to it, ordered by the strength of their co-occurrence. This value is a measure of how often the focal keyword and a particular neighbour appear together in the publication metadata. For example, searching for the keyword term “health” in this table reveals that “health” and “canada” co-occur 9 times in this dataset.
The Community profiles table provides a compact overview of the vocabulary associated with each intellectual community.
The Community vocabulary table lists every keyword in the network by community, allowing readers to move beyond the most prominent terms and examine more specialized areas that may be difficult to identify visually. The Community profiles and Community vocabulary look up tables provide insight into the structure of these communities. The keyword “health”, for examples belongs to community two and has a rank 12, indicating that it is the twelfth most commonly connected term in this research commuinity.

The tables report each keyword’s rank and degree.2
In the spirit of “member checking” (Birt et al. 2016; McKim 2023), I am curious how you might label these communities. Based on your understanding of your own scholarly activity and the keyword clusters, what would be a reasonable description of one, some, or all of these communities?

title: Institutional Research Network
text:
This bibliometric study examines 36 years of SMU-affiliated research, from January 1990 through December 2025. The corpus is restricted to publications for which the institutional affiliation metadata explicitly identifies SMU. No restrictions were placed on document type. These deliberately broad parameters were intended to capture the full range of scholarly outputs indexed by Web of Science (WoS) that can be attributed to faculty, staff, and researchers associated with SMU, providing a basis for examining publication behaviour, research activity, and patterns of connection and collaboration across the university community over the period.
The search produced a corpus of 7,850 publications appearing across 2,862 different publication sources, reflecting a wide range of scholarly venues and the disciplinary breadth of the university. The corpus should not, however, be treated as a complete inventory of everything produced at SMU. Web of Science is widely used for bibliometric research, but, like all bibliographic databases, it is selective. Its coverage tends to favour English-language journals and disciplines in which journal articles and collaborative publication are dominant forms of scholarly communication. Fields in which research is more often communicated through books, book chapters, regional journals, professional publications, or other locally oriented venues may therefore be less completely represented. This is particularly consequential for some areas of the humanities and social sciences. The analysis should accordingly be understood as a description of the SMU research activity visible through Web of Science rather than an exhaustive account of the university’s entire research culture.

title: Institutional Research Network
text:
What the keyword network shows
The keyword co-occurrence network provides one way of examining the internal structure of this corpus. Rather than treating the 7,850 publications simply as a collection of separate outputs, the network asks how the keywords used to describe those publications are connected to one another. Each node represents a keyword, and a connection between two nodes indicates that the two keywords occur together in the metadata for at least one publication. The network therefore shows not only which topics are present in the corpus, but how those topics are connected. Keywords connected to many other terms are more extensively embedded in the wider research network, while keywords with fewer connections tend to occupy more specialized positions.
Patterns of connectedness are especially important. When groups of keywords are more densely connected to one another than to the rest of the network, they form what can reasonably be described as intellectual communities. Represented by colour in the visualization, these communities are not predetermined departments, disciplines, or administrative categories. Rather, they are emergent groupings of connected concepts, research problems, methods, populations, and objects of study that recur together across the publication corpus. In this sense, the network provides a map of the scholarly activity represented in the corpus: not only what SMU researchers study, but how that activity is intellectually connected. It shows which topics repeatedly appear together, where areas of research overlap, which topics connect otherwise distinct areas, and which occupy more specialized positions within the broader research landscape.
A connection does not imply that two concepts have the same meaning or necessarily belong to the same discipline. It indicates a bibliographic relationship: the terms have been used together in describing the same scholarly output. The network is therefore best read as a map of research connectedness and association within the indexed corpus.

title: Institutional Research Network
text:
What a keyword represents
The network combines two forms of keyword metadata: author keywords and database-generated keywords. Author keywords are terms selected by authors to describe the subject matter of their own publication. Database-generated keywords, such as Keywords Plus, are generated from information in the bibliographic record and are intended to identify additional topical relationships. The two forms were combined before constructing the network so that the analysis could draw on a broader representation of the subjects and concepts associated with each publication.
When a reader sees a node labelled migration, galaxies, education, or another term, the node does not represent a researcher, department, publication, or project. It represents a term occurring in the bibliographic description of the research corpus. What matters analytically is not simply whether that term appears, but its pattern of connection to other terms. A keyword may be highly connected because it occurs alongside many different topics across the corpus, or it may be comparatively specialized because its connections are concentrated within a narrower area of research.
The vocabulary itself is heterogeneous. Some keywords identify broad substantive areas, while others identify theoretical concepts, research methods, populations, geographic locations, objects of study, scientific processes, or highly specialized phenomena. Because author-supplied and database-generated keywords are combined, the network should be interpreted as a representation of how SMU research is bibliographically described and connected rather than as a direct inventory of the concepts researchers themselves would necessarily identify as most important.

section: How to use the network and tables
text:
How to use the network and tables
The interactive network provides the broadest view of these relationships. Use the keyword search above the network to locate a particular term. Selecting a keyword highlights its node in yellow with a black border. Once selected, the nodes connected directly to that keyword are also highlighted. The network can then be zoomed and panned to bring these linked nodes into focus, and individual nodes may be dragged to make crowded areas easier to inspect. Moving a node changes only its position on the screen and does not alter the underlying network analysis.
When you look at a keyword together with all of its neighbours, you are looking at that keyword’s immediate local network. The selected keyword is the focal term, and each neighbour is another keyword that appeared with it in the metadata of at least one publication in the corpus. The neighbourhood therefore shows the set of topics, concepts, methods, populations, places, or objects of study that have been directly associated with that keyword in SMU-affiliated research. This neighbourhood can be interpreted as a picture of the keyword’s intellectual context. A keyword with neighbours drawn largely from one community is embedded mainly within a relatively concentrated area of research. Selecting the keywords “behaviour”, “radial velocities”, “health”, “management history”, or “actor network theory” from the keyword drop down search menu offers an illustration of this type of pattern. A keyword whose neighbours span several communities may instead connect otherwise distinct areas of scholarly activity. Selecting the keywords “origin”, “sequence”, or “evolution” will illustrate this type of pattern.
Node colour identifies community membership. Nodes with the same colour belong to the same intellectual community. Node size represents degree of connectedness: larger nodes are directly connected to a greater number of other keywords in the network, while smaller nodes have fewer direct connections and tend to occupy more specialized positions. Node size therefore represents network connectedness rather than the quality, importance, or volume of research associated with a keyword.
The tables provide complementary ways of examining the same network. The Keyword Neighbours table allows a reader to select an exact keyword and retrieve all of the terms directly connected to it, ordered by the strength of their co-occurrence. This value is a measure of how often the focal keyword and a particular neighbour appear together in the publication metadata. For example, searching for the keyword term “health” in this table reveals that “health” and “canada” co-occur 9 times in this dataset. The Community Profiles table provides a compact overview of the vocabulary associated with each intellectual community. The Community Vocabulary table lists every keyword in the network by community, allowing readers to move beyond the most prominent terms and examine more specialized areas that may be difficult to identify visually. The Community profiles and Community vocabulary look up tables provide insight into the structure of these communities. The keyword “health”, for examples belongs to community two and has a rank 12, indicating that it is the twelfth most commonly connected term in this research commuinity.
The tables report each keyword’s rank and degree.1
In the spirit of “member checking” (Birt et al. 2016; McKim 2023), I am curious how you might label these communities. Based on your understanding of your own scholarly activity and the keyword clusters, what would be a reasonable description of one, some, or all of these communities?

title: Describing the SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
Academic Managerialism
The introduction of corporate steering in public research sectors is frequently framed as a necessary mechanism to increase operational efficiency and institutional accountability. Scholars examining the Central and Eastern European contexts demonstrate that department heads are forced to act as primary mediators, negotiating the friction between emerging corporate managerial expectations and traditional academic autonomy (Machovcova, Zabrodska, and Mudrak 2019). This transition shifts the university from an open site of unconstrained intellectual inquiry to a managed environment where output is being both quantified and regularised. Empirical observations of these policy shifts suggest that while they aim to stimulate public research efficiency, they can function as a double-edged sword, leading to administrative inflation and narrow publishing strategies among faculty (Schubert 2009).
The global reach of these corporate practices is evident across diverse higher education landscapes, including developing regions such as the United Arab Emirates, where new managerialism is deployed to reshape institutional reputations (Ajayan and Balasubramanian 2020). When fiscal cutbacks occur, the pressure to maintain research performance becomes even more acute; institutions are forced to sustain or accelerate output levels even when financial incentives and direct support is declines (Bak and Kim 2023). At the core of this management system is the corporate premise that academic institutions are structurally no different from any commercial enterprise and can therefore be optimised through auditing and performance-monitoring systems (Hasham 2018). Consequently, the historical evolution of research performance measurement systems, particularly within heavily evaluated sectors like Australian higher education, outlines a steady intensification of administrative oversight (Martin-Sardesai et al. 2019).

section: Institutional Leadership and Strategic Shared Visions
text:
Institutional Leadership and Strategic Shared Visions
A central tenet of corporate strategic planning is that institutional leadership is in a position to steer research excellence. Recent quantitative modeling of presidential capabilities in Chinese higher education argues that specific strategic competencies at the executive level correlate positively with institutional performance gains and international visibility (Dong, Wu, and Yu 2025). Similarly, evaluations of academic leadership and university performance across European and Russian contexts investigate whether universities demonstrate measurable improvements when led by active, highly cited scholars who embody research excellence, rather than pure career administrators (Gerashchenko 2022). This structural steering is frequently reinforced by regional contagion effects, where the strategic choices and performance trajectories of neighbouring peer institutions create a normative pressure that drives local academic leadership to adopt identical strategic management models (Saftiuc, Proscanu, and Teodorescu 2025).
For these administrative plans to translate into scholarly output, university leaders direct attention to building an institutional shared vision that attempts to bridge the historical divide between research and teaching mandates (Bui et al. 2024). Senior management relies on transformational leadership styles, operating under the assumption that inspiring a collective corporate identity will foster internal creativity and outputs (Salim and Zakaria 2021). In fields such as green innovation and technology transfer, evidence indicates that the specific academic and corporate experiences of the top management team can shape the volume and direction of institutional innovation outputs (Zhao et al. 2021). Moreover, when academic executives retain active boardroom connections, they can connect lab-based research with high-impact industrial commercialisation, demonstrating how top-down strategies attempt to steer basic science toward applied economic utility (Zhu, Wu, and Gaidai 2025).

title: Describing the SMU-affiliated Research Corpus
text:
Guiding Research Productivity
At the level of the faculty member, the primary mechanisms used to enforce strategic alignment are institutional incentives, formal performance appraisals, and individual research productivity tracking. Evidence suggests that while structured interventions can alter short-term output counts, they rarely change long-term scholarly trajectories (Ryazanova and Jaskiene 2022). While routine bibliometric reports are frequently positioned as one tool among many, these data summaries often function as coercive monitoring mechanisms that hold individual faculty accountable to generic performance targets (Cabezas-Clavijo and Torres-Salinas 2021). In some cases, advanced institutional frameworks have emerged, such as bibliometric strength, potential, and risk analysis models, which allow administrators to track exactly how faculty publication choices respond to central strategic choices and funding pathways (Iping et al. 2024).
The efficacy of these incentive structures remains dependent on localized professional contexts and personal scholarly investments. In Canada, broad empirical studies of primary care researchers demonstrate that productivity is strongly associated with protected research time, dedicated infrastructure, and targeted team-based funding rather than purely top-down corporate mandates (Aggarwal et al. 2024). Furthermore, the specialized nature of research production is heavily reliant on specific cognitive resources and long-term personal investments, which means that arbitrary administrative redirections can result in cognitive friction and operational inefficiency for the scholar (Degli Antoni, Fia, and Sacconi 2022). Quantitative analyses of individual academic research agendas confirm that broader organizational factors and institutional priorities interact directly with disciplinary traditions, meaning that top-down steering tools must constantly compete with an academic’s internalized scholarly values and peer networks (Horta and Santos 2020).

text:
Tensions, Resistance, and Academic Freedom
The imposition of corporate performance management has generated tensions, with many scholars arguing that these frameworks stifle academic freedom and distort genuine knowledge production. Critical discourse analyses highlight that aggressive performance management frameworks force a precarious state of affairs upon academic work, transforming scholarly writing into a rushed commodity designed to satisfy auditing cycles rather than solve profound intellectual problems (Morrish and Sauntson 2016). This shift creates a sense of alienation, where academic identities are systematically reconfigured to fit the parameters of the managed university, sparking widespread subtle resistance among faculty who seek to protect their professional autonomy from neoliberal encroachment (Morrish 2017). In specialized fields like social work education, the imposition of a marketized, neo-liberal agenda is shown to directly compromise the critical, social-justice mission of the discipline by prioritizing commercial metric capture over community engagement (MacDonald and Nixon 2016).
The human cost of these auditing regimes is captured in qualitative terms by academics who describe the modern pressure cooker environment (Xu and Poole 2024). This creates institutional struggles for recognition where individual departments are pitted against one another for scarce resources, fragmenting the university’s traditional community of scholars (Muench and Baier 2012). Moreover, the formal policies and administrative structures often lack meaningful faculty buy-in because they are perceived as top-down compliance exercises rather than authentic scholarly transformations (Castro-Gomez et al. 2026). Without aligning internal policy incentives directly with the intrinsic motivations and professional values of the faculty, centralized administrative mandates fail to cultivate genuine participation or sustainable scholarly growth (Barsallo et al. 2026).

Do Strategic Research Plans Work?
This breief review on higher education management demonstrates a conflict between top-down corporate steering and bottom-up faculty behaviour. While institutional theories and administrative models posit that clear leadership capabilities, shared corporate visions, and targeted bibliometric monitoring can successfully optimize and direct an institution’s research performance, empirical accounts expose resistance, strategic gaming, and profound alignment failures. This contradiction exposes a gap in evaluative scientometrics: we lack robust, objective, longitudinal measures of whether corporate university strategies genuinely shape the intellectual landscape of an institution or if they merely retroactively rebrand pre-existing, faculty-driven strengths.
It is with this in mind that I raise the following question: do strategic research plans work?
I explore this question turning to the research corpus of Saint Mary’s University (SMU).
